text: Your browser finds websites by looking up their addresses through DNS resolution, which happens every time you type a web address. It starts with a check of the browser cache, where recently visited sites are stored. If the address isn't there, the request goes to a recursive resolver. The resolver asks a root server where to look, gets pointed to the right top-level domain server (like .com or .org), and finally reaches the authoritative server, which holds the exact address for the site. The resolver then hands the answer back to your device and stores it for a while. The TTL, or time to live, controls how long that lasts, typically about 300 seconds, so the next visit is faster. All of this takes a fraction of a second.
